title: Grade 4 CREATIVE ARTS — 3.1 Analysis of Creative Arts Works

pages.lesson:
PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Appreciation means looking, listening and responding to Creative Arts with care. In this sub-strand you will explain what appreciation includes, make a portfolio for your artworks, and study the Kenya National Anthem and a Kenyan folk song. You will also take part in games and sports and talk about teamwork, safety and works from different cultures.

## Strand 3.0: Appreciation in Creative Arts
Sub-strand 3.1: Analysis of Creative Arts Works
Suggested lessons: 15

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) explain the concept of appreciation in Creative Arts
b) make a portfolio for presenting creative art works
c) analyse the Kenya National Anthem to foster patriotism
d) describe a Kenyan folk song performance using appropriate terminologies
e) participate in games and sports within the school for enjoyment
f) value appreciation of Creative Arts works drawn from various cultural backgrounds

## What this sub-strand covers
• Making a portfolio
• Concept of appreciation: appropriate behaviour, aesthetic, skills, message communicated, how to give feedback, care of displayed works
• Kenya National Anthem; role, values, occasions and number of verses performed
• Components of a folk song: community of origin Type/ occasion, Message, participants and their roles (soloist, instrumentalist, singers), instruments

## Key inquiry questions
1. What is the importance of analysis in Creative Arts?

## Core competencies
• Citizenship: The learner gets to appreciate Kenyan music as they listen to and analyse Kenyan National Anthem and folk songs
• Learning to learn: The learner gets to interact with different type of Creative Arts works gaining new knowledge
• Digital Literacy: The learner appreciates different works of art displayed through multimedia

## Values
• Unity: The learner collaborates with others when analysing in groups the execution of sports skills
• Respect: The learner appreciates others while analysing Creative Arts works in groups
• Integrity: The learner observes sportsmanship during mini games
• Patriotism: The learner develops the love for Kenya as they discuss aspects of the Kenya National Anthem

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Health and safety: The learner participates in sports activities for enjoyment and fun
• Social cohesion: The learner analyses in groups the execution of sports skills in inter class/inter school championships
• Analytical and creative thinking: The learner analyses music and sports events and critiques art works
• Cultural awareness: The learner analyses folk songs from different parts of the Kenya

## Links to other learning areas
• Social Studies: The learner integrates with others while undertaking various tasks in groups
• English: The learner enhances their listening and speaking skills in English while discussing the music listened to

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Creative Arts Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 3.0 Appreciation in Creative Arts, Sub-strand 3.1 Analysis of Creative Arts Works

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: What appreciation means

LESSON 1: WHAT APPRECIATION MEANS
=================================

## What you will learn
• Explain appreciation in Creative Arts.
• Name the parts of appreciation: behaviour, beauty, skill, message, feedback and care.
• Show appropriate behaviour while looking at or listening to a work.

Curriculum outcomes: a) explain the concept of appreciation in Creative Arts

## Introduction
Finishing a picture, a song or a race is not the last step. Someone has to look or listen properly. That careful attention, and the fair words that follow it, is appreciation.

## Notes
Appreciation in Creative Arts means giving a work your full attention and responding to it with respect. The work might be a drawing, a painting, a photograph, a song, a folk dance or a sports performance. Analysis is the part of appreciation where you separate the work into pieces so you can understand it. Analysis matters because it helps you see the message, improve your own work, and respect the person who made or performed the work.

In this sub-strand, appreciation includes six ideas.

- **Appropriate behaviour:** sit or stand where you can see and hear. Do not touch a display unless you are allowed to. Do not talk over a song. Do not laugh at a performer.
- **Aesthetic:** the beauty and organisation of the work, such as colour, neatness, balance and a pleasing sound.
- **Skills:** what the maker or performer was able to do, such as a steady balance, a clean pitch or a well-lit photograph.
- **Message:** what the work is communicating.
- **Feedback:** comments that help, given kindly.
- **Care of displayed works:** keeping artworks clean, dry and unharmed.

You do not have to like everything. Appreciation is not pretending. It is being able to say what you noticed and why, without insulting the maker. A useful sentence is: “I notice… and it makes me think…”

When the class listens to a short song or looks at a painting, fold your arms or rest your hands so you are not tempted to touch. Wait until the work is finished. Then speak. That behaviour is the doorway to every other kind of appreciation.

## Key words
• appreciation — giving a work full attention and responding with respect
• analysis — looking at the parts of a work so you can understand it
• aesthetic — to do with beauty and how pleasing a work looks or sounds

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner talks all through a folk song and then says they appreciated it. What is missing?

Working:
1. Appreciation includes appropriate behaviour.
2. Talking over the song means they did not attend to it.

Answer: Appropriate behaviour. They did not listen, so they cannot yet claim to have appreciated the song.

### Example 2
Why is analysis useful?

Working:
1. Analysis separates a work into parts.
2. Those parts reveal the message and the skills.

Answer: It helps you understand the message, improve your own work and respect the maker.

## Activity: Attend, then speak
You will need: One displayed picture and one short recorded song, Exercise books
1. Brainstorm what appreciation means and list the six ideas.
2. Look at the picture in silence for one minute. Do not touch it.
3. Listen to the song in silence.
4. Write “I notice… and it makes me think…” for each work.
5. Share one sentence and let the next person finish before you speak.

## Practice
1. What is appreciation in Creative Arts?
2. Name three things appreciation includes.
3. Why is analysis important?

## Summary
• Appreciation is careful attention and a respectful response.
• It includes behaviour, beauty, skill, message, feedback and care.
• Analysis helps you understand a work instead of only saying you like it.

### Answers to practice
1. Giving a work your full attention and responding to it with respect.
2. Any three: appropriate behaviour, aesthetic qualities, skills, message, feedback, care of displayed works.
3. It helps you understand the message, improve your own work and respect the maker or performer.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Aesthetic qualities, skills and message

LESSON 2: AESTHETIC QUALITIES, SKILLS AND MESSAGE
=================================================

## What you will learn
• Comment on the look or sound of a work.
• Name a skill used to make or perform it.
• Suggest a message the work communicates.

Curriculum outcomes: a) explain the concept of appreciation in Creative Arts

## Introduction
“It is nice” does not tell a painter, a singer or a runner anything they can use. Separating beauty, skill and message gives you something true to say.

## Notes
Use three questions on any Creative Arts work.

### What is aesthetic here?
Aesthetic questions are about the senses. In a picture: Are the colours clear? Is the work neat? Is there a balance between the parts? In a photograph: Is the light helping, and is the centre of interest easy to see? In music: Is the tone pleasant? Do the voices match? In gymnastics or sport: Is the body shape clear and controlled? You are describing beauty and organisation, not guessing the price of the work.

### What skill was used?
Skill is what someone has learnt to do. A neat Kenyan flag shows painting skill and knowledge of colour order. A side roll in a straight line shows body control. A recorder melody on B, A and G shows fingering and breath. A pass in netball shows eye and hand skill. Name the skill you can actually see or hear. Do not praise a skill that was not in the performance.

### What message is communicated?
The message is the idea the work carries. A topical song may say “keep the compound clean”. The national anthem carries a message of unity and service. A folk song may advise, mourn, celebrate or call people to work. A sports performance can communicate teamwork even without words. If you are not sure of the message, say “I think the message is…” and give your reason.

Write the three answers in a table with the headings Aesthetic, Skill and Message. A full appreciation uses all three columns. One column alone is only a fragment.

Respect the limits of what you know. If a song is in a language you do not understand, you may comment on the sound, the skill and the occasion, and ask someone from that community about the message instead of inventing it.

## Key words
• skill — something a person has learnt to do well
• message — the idea a work communicates

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A photograph shows a well-lit pot in the middle of a plain background. Give one aesthetic comment and one skill comment.

Working:
1. Aesthetic comments describe look.
2. Skill comments describe what the photographer managed to do.

Answer: Aesthetic: the pot is clear and the background is calm. Skill: the photographer used light and chose a centre of interest.

### Example 2
Learners laugh at the words of a song they do not understand and invent a rude meaning. What should they do instead?

Working:
1. Do not invent a message.
2. Ask someone who knows the language.

Answer: Comment on the sound and the skill, and ask a person from that community what the song means.

## Activity: Three-column analysis
You will need: A displayed artwork, A short performance or recording, A table with three columns
1. Choose one artwork and one performance.
2. Fill Aesthetic, Skill and Message for each.
3. Compare tables with a partner and change any comment that has no evidence.
4. Underline the comment you are most sure of.
5. Ask one question about anything you could not interpret.

## Practice
1. What kind of comment is “the colours are neat and the shapes are balanced”?
2. What is the difference between a skill and a message?
3. What should you do if you do not understand the language of a song?

## Summary
• Ask what is beautiful or well organised, what skill was used, and what message is carried.
• Base each answer on something you can see or hear.
• Do not invent a meaning for a language you do not know.

### Answers to practice
1. An aesthetic comment.
2. A skill is what the person is able to do. A message is the idea the work communicates.
3. Do not invent the meaning. Comment on what you can hear and ask someone who knows the language.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Feedback and care of displayed works

LESSON 3: FEEDBACK AND CARE OF DISPLAYED WORKS
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Give feedback that is kind, specific and useful.
• Show how to care for works on display.
• Explain why works from different cultures deserve the same care.

Curriculum outcomes: a) explain the concept of appreciation in Creative Arts; f) value appreciation of Creative Arts works drawn from various cultural backgrounds

## Introduction
Feedback can help a classmate improve, or it can make them never want to show work again. Care of a display can keep a painting alive for the whole school, or destroy it in a minute.

## Notes
### How to give feedback
Use this order.

1. Say what you noticed, using aesthetic quality, skill or message.
2. Say what worked.
3. Offer one suggestion, not a list of five.
4. Stop talking and let the maker reply.

A strong example: “I noticed a straight side roll. The body control worked well. Next time, hold the crab balance a little longer.”

A weak example: “It was bad.” It has no detail and no respect.

Do not compare a learner cruelly with a friend. Do not shout feedback across the room. In a group, each person speaks once before anyone speaks twice. That fairness is part of respect.

### Care of displayed works
- Dry paintings before they are stacked.
- Handle paper by the edges.
- Do not write on someone else’s work.
- Keep water, food and dirty hands away from displays.
- Fasten work with tape or clips that the teacher provides, not with pins through the middle of a picture.
- Put sculptures and portfolios where they will not be kicked.
- If you must move a display, ask first.

### Different cultural backgrounds
A painting of a community ceremony, a folk song, or a game from another Kenyan community is not less important than work from your own. Care and feedback stay the same. Laughing at clothing, language or style in a display is not analysis. Valuing works from many backgrounds means you give them the same silence, the same careful hands and the same honest, kind words.

Write one feedback comment you would be willing to hear about your own work. If you would not want to hear it, do not say it to someone else.

## Key words
• feedback — a response that says what worked and one way to improve
• display — work put where others can see it

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Rewrite “Your flag is messy and silly” as useful feedback.

Working:
1. Notice one real point.
2. Say what worked, then one suggestion.

Answer: Example: “I noticed the three wide stripes. The black stripe at the top works. Next time, let each colour dry so the edges stay neat.”

### Example 2
A learner pins a drawing through the middle so it will not fall. What is the problem?

Working:
1. The pin damages the work.
2. Edges or clips should be used instead.

Answer: The pin makes a hole in the picture. Fasten it at the edges or ask the teacher for a clip.

## Activity: Feedback and a safe display
You will need: Two artworks or photographs, Space to display them, Clips or tape
1. Display the works without damaging them.
2. Each learner gives one feedback comment using the four-step order.
3. The maker replies with “thank you” and may ask one question.
4. Check hands are clean and the works are away from food and water.
5. Discuss how you would give the same care to a work from a community that is not your own.

## Practice
1. What are the four steps of useful feedback?
2. Give two ways to care for a displayed painting.
3. Why should works from another culture receive the same care?

## Summary
• Feedback notices something, names a strength and offers one suggestion.
• Handle displays by the edges and keep them clean and dry.
• Give the same respect to works from every cultural background.

### Answers to practice
1. Say what you noticed, say what worked, offer one suggestion, and let the maker reply.
2. Any two: let it dry, handle the edges, keep food and water away, do not write on it, do not pin through the middle.
3. They are equally worth respecting. Appreciation does not rank communities.

PAGE 5: Lesson 4: Making a portfolio

LESSON 4: MAKING A PORTFOLIO
============================

## What you will learn
• Explain what a portfolio is for.
• Make a simple portfolio from local materials.
• Decorate it and place artwork inside without damage.

Curriculum outcomes: b) make a portfolio for presenting creative art works

## Introduction
Loose drawings in a desk get torn, and nobody can find the one worth showing. A portfolio is a made container that keeps Creative Arts work together and ready to present.

## Notes
A portfolio is a folder or case that holds your Creative Arts work. A **working portfolio** collects work while you are still learning: sketches, photographs, notes and unfinished ideas. A **display portfolio** holds the work you have chosen to show. In Grade 4 you can make one strong folder that does both jobs.

### Materials
Use what is available: a large piece of manila paper, two pieces of cardboard from a clean box, or a folded chart. You also need glue or tape, and coloured paper or scraps of fabric for decoration. Do not cut up a book or someone else’s work to get the cardboard.

### Steps
1. Cut or fold the cover so it is bigger than the artwork. A folder that is too small bends the pictures.
2. Join the sides and the bottom, and leave the top open. If you glue the top as well, you cannot get the work in.
3. Decorate the front by pasting coloured paper or fabric. Leave a space to write your name, your class and the words “Creative Arts portfolio”.
4. Let the glue dry before you put work inside.
5. Slide artwork in carefully. A painting must be dry. A photograph should be flat.
6. You may write a small label on a separate strip: “Kenyan flag, painted in class”, not across the picture itself.

### Presenting
When you present the portfolio, take out one work at a time, say its title, and use the appreciation language you have learnt. Then put it back. Do not empty the folder onto the floor.

A portfolio shows responsibility. It also lets a teacher see progress, because early work and later work can sit together. Care for it as you care for a display: clean hands, no food inside, and a safe shelf.

## Key words
• portfolio — a folder that keeps and presents Creative Arts work
• working portfolio — a collection of work still in progress
• display portfolio — a collection of work chosen to be shown

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner glues all four edges of the folder. What goes wrong?

Working:
1. The artwork has to go in through an opening.
2. Gluing every edge leaves no opening.

Answer: There is no way to put the artwork inside. One edge, usually the top, must stay open.

### Example 2
The cover is 30 cm wide and the painting is 34 cm wide. Will the painting fit without bending?

Working:
1. 34 is greater than 30.
2. The cover needs to be bigger than the work.

Answer: No. The cover is smaller than the painting, so the painting would bend.

## Activity: Build and fill a portfolio
You will need: Manila paper or clean cardboard, Glue or tape, Coloured paper or fabric scraps, Dry artwork
1. Make a folder bigger than your artwork, with the top open.
2. Decorate the front with coloured paper or fabric and write your name.
3. Let it dry.
4. Place one dry artwork inside and add a separate label.
5. Present that one work to a partner, then return it to the portfolio.

## Practice
1. What is a portfolio for?
2. Which edge of a simple folder should stay open?
3. When is it safe to put a painting into the portfolio?

## Summary
• A portfolio keeps work and helps you present it.
• Make it from local materials, decorate it, and leave an opening.
• Put in dry, flat work and handle it with clean hands.

### Answers to practice
1. To keep Creative Arts work safe and to present chosen work.
2. The top, so artwork can go in.
3. When the paint is dry.

PAGE 6: Lesson 5: The Kenya National Anthem: role, occasions and verses

LESSON 5: THE KENYA NATIONAL ANTHEM: ROLE, OCCASIONS AND VERSES
============================================================

## What you will learn
• State the role of the Kenya National Anthem.
• Name occasions when it is performed.
• Recognise that a full performance has three verses.

Curriculum outcomes: c) analyse the Kenya National Anthem to foster patriotism

## Introduction
When the Kenya National Anthem begins, people stand. That habit has a reason. The anthem is one of the ways the country recognises itself.

## Notes
The Kenya National Anthem is the official patriotic song of Kenya. Its Kiswahili title is Ee Mungu Nguvu Yetu. The tune comes from a traditional Pokomo lullaby. The anthem was adopted in 1963, when Kenya became independent. It is sung in Kiswahili and in English.

### Role
The anthem identifies the nation. It asks for blessing, justice, unity, peace and plenty, and it calls citizens to serve and to build the country. Standing for it shows respect. It is a sign of patriotism, not background music.

### Occasions
It is performed at school assemblies, at flag-raising ceremonies, on national days, and when Kenya is represented at international events. National days include Madaraka Day on 1 June, Mashujaa Day on 20 October and Jamhuri Day on 12 December.

### Three verses
A full performance has **three verses**. Each verse has six lines. Some assemblies sing the first verse when time is short, but you should know that the complete anthem has three, and you should be able to listen to all three with attention.

**Verse 1** is a prayer: “O God of all creation, bless this our land and nation…” It asks for justice, unity, peace, liberty and plenty.

**Verse 2** calls everyone to service: “Let one and all arise with hearts both strong and true…” It speaks of defending the homeland.

**Verse 3** calls people to build the nation together and to be thankful: “Let all with one accord in common bond united…”

### Behaviour
Stand still, face the flag if there is one, and stop talking before the first note. Caps come off. You sing if you know the words, or you stand in respectful silence. You do not walk, chew or laugh. When the three verses end, you wait for the signal before you move. That behaviour is part of analysing the anthem as a national symbol, not only as a tune.

## Key words
• national anthem — the official patriotic song of a country
• verse — one section of a song
• patriotism — love and respect for one’s country

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A performance includes verse 1 and verse 2 only. How many verses of the full anthem were left out?

Working:
1. The full anthem has 3 verses.
2. 3 − 2 = 1

Answer: 1

### Example 2
On which date is Jamhuri Day?

Working:
1. Jamhuri Day is a known national day.
2. It is 12 December.

Answer: 12 December.

## Activity: Listen to the three verses
You will need: A recording or a live singing of all three verses of the Kenya National Anthem, The flag if the school has one
1. Stand in silence and listen to all three verses.
2. After the anthem, sit and say what each verse is mainly about.
3. List two occasions when the anthem is performed.
4. Discuss the role it plays for the country.
5. Practise the correct standing position once more as the first verse is played.

## Practice
1. How many verses does the full Kenya National Anthem have?
2. Give two occasions when it is performed.
3. What is one role of the anthem?

## Summary
• The anthem is Kenya’s official patriotic song, adopted in 1963.
• A full performance has three verses.
• Stand still and give it your attention on national and school occasions.

### Answers to practice
1. Three.
2. Any two: school assemblies, flag ceremonies, Madaraka Day, Mashujaa Day, Jamhuri Day, international events where Kenya is represented.
3. It identifies the nation and expresses patriotism, unity and respect.

PAGE 7: Lesson 6: Values in the Kenya National Anthem

LESSON 6: VALUES IN THE KENYA NATIONAL ANTHEM
=============================================

## What you will learn
• Find values named in the three verses.
• Explain how those values build patriotism.
• Connect one value to behaviour at school.

Curriculum outcomes: c) analyse the Kenya National Anthem to foster patriotism

## Introduction
The anthem is not only a tune to stand up for. Its words tell citizens how to live with one another. Finding those values is analysis.

## Notes
Listen again, this time for values. A value is a belief about what is right and worth protecting.

### Verse 1
The prayer asks for **justice** (“Justice be our shield and defender”), **unity** (“May we dwell in unity”), **peace**, **liberty** and **plenty**. Justice means fairness. Unity means staying together. Peace means living without harming one another. Liberty means freedom. Plenty means enough for people to live.

### Verse 2
“Service be our earnest endeavour” names **service**, which is working for others and for the country. “Firm may we stand to defend” names **courage** and responsibility for the homeland. The verse asks for strong, true hearts. That is sincerity, not showing off.

### Verse 3
“In common bond united” returns to unity. “Build this our nation together” names **hard work** and cooperation. “Fill every heart with thanksgiving” names **gratitude**. The glory of the country is described as the fruit of labour, so the anthem does not promise pride without effort.

Taken together, the anthem fosters patriotism by giving love of country a practical meaning: be fair, stay united, keep the peace, serve, work and be thankful.

### At school
You practise these values in small ways. Unity is singing together and playing as a team. Justice is taking turns. Service is tidying the space after art or games. Peace is refusing to mock a performance. Gratitude is thanking the person who taught you a song. Patriotism is standing properly for the anthem and treating the flag with care.

When you analyse the anthem, quote or point to the line that carries the value. “I like verse 2” is an opinion. “Verse 2 asks for service” is analysis.

## Key words
• value — a belief about what is right and worth protecting
• justice — fairness
• unity — being together as one people

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which value is clearest in the line “May we dwell in unity”?

Working:
1. The line uses the word unity.
2. Dwelling in unity means living together as one.

Answer: Unity.

### Example 2
A learner says verse 3 is about thanksgiving but cannot point to a line. What should they add?

Working:
1. Analysis points to the words.
2. Verse 3 speaks of filling every heart with thanksgiving.

Answer: They should point to the line about filling every heart with thanksgiving.

## Activity: Match lines to values
You will need: The three verses written where the class can see them, Cards labelled Unity, Justice, Service, Hard work, Thanksgiving, Peace
1. Listen to or read the three verses again.
2. In groups, match each value card to a line.
3. Explain the match in one sentence.
4. Choose one value and say how you can practise it at school this week.
5. Stand and sing or listen to verse 1 with the value of unity in mind.

## Practice
1. Name three values found in the Kenya National Anthem.
2. Which verse especially calls people to serve and defend the homeland?
3. Give one way to practise unity at school.

## Summary
• Verse 1 prays for justice, unity, peace, liberty and plenty.
• Verse 2 calls for service. Verse 3 calls for shared work and thanksgiving.
• Patriotism here means living those values, including at school.

### Answers to practice
1. Any three: justice, unity, peace, liberty, service, hard work, gratitude or thanksgiving, patriotism.
2. Verse 2.
3. Any one: sing together, take turns, play as a team, listen to one another.

PAGE 8: Lesson 7: Describing a Kenyan folk song

LESSON 7: DESCRIBING A KENYAN FOLK SONG
=======================================

## What you will learn
• Describe a folk song using community, occasion, message, participants and instruments.
• Use the words soloist, instrumentalist and singers correctly.
• Avoid guessing facts you did not see or hear.

Curriculum outcomes: d) describe a Kenyan folk song performance using appropriate terminologies

## Introduction
A good description of a folk song is like a good description of a match. You name who took part, what they did, and what the event was for. Feelings come after the facts.

## Notes
When you analyse a Kenyan folk song performance, use these components.

- **Community of origin:** which community the song comes from. If you do not know, write “not yet identified” and ask. Do not guess from the costumes alone.
- **Type or occasion:** work, funeral, naming, initiation, marriage, worship, or another occasion you can support from the performance or from a reliable person.
- **Message:** what the song is saying or doing for the people at that occasion. Ask if the language is not yours.
- **Participants and their roles:** the **soloist** leads, the **singers** answer or join the tune, and the **instrumentalist** plays. One person might dance as well. Name the roles you actually saw.
- **Instruments:** drums, kayamba, shakers, or body percussion such as clapping. Name only the instruments you heard.

A clear description sounds like this: “This was isukuti from Luhya communities, especially associated with the Isukha and Idakho. It is performed at joyful occasions such as weddings. I saw drummers, who were the instrumentalists, and dancers who also sang. The message I could confirm is celebration. I would need a speaker of the language to explain every line.”

That is appropriate terminology. Words such as “nice”, “funny clothes” or “noise” are not analysis.

Compare two songs only when you have the components for both. You may find that a work song and a marriage song use different speeds and different messages, and that both deserve respect. Cultural awareness grows when the description is accurate.

## Key words
• soloist — the person who leads the singing
• instrumentalist — the person who plays an instrument
• community of origin — the community the song comes from

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A report says, “The song was noisy and from somewhere.” What is missing?

Working:
1. A description needs components.
2. Community, occasion, roles and instruments are missing, and the tone is disrespectful.

Answer: It does not name the community, the occasion, the message, the roles or the instruments.

### Example 2
Three people hit drums and one person leads the singing while ten people answer. Who is the soloist?

Working:
1. The soloist leads the singing.
2. The drummers are instrumentalists.

Answer: The person who leads the singing.

## Activity: Analyse one performance
You will need: A live or recorded Kenyan folk song, A component chart
1. Watch or listen once without writing.
2. Watch again and fill: community, occasion, message, soloist, singers, instrumentalists, instruments.
3. Leave a box blank rather than guessing.
4. Share the chart with another group and challenge any fact that was not in the performance.
5. Write two sentences of appreciation using the correct terms.

## Practice
1. List five components used to describe a folk song performance.
2. What does the instrumentalist do?
3. What should you write if you do not know the community of origin?

## Summary
• Describe community, occasion, message, roles and instruments.
• Use the terms soloist, singers and instrumentalist.
• Leave out any fact you cannot support.

### Answers to practice
1. Community of origin, type or occasion, message, participants and their roles, and instruments.
2. Plays an instrument.
3. “Not yet identified,” and then ask. Do not guess.

PAGE 9: Lesson 8: Games, sports and respect for many cultures

LESSON 8: GAMES, SPORTS AND RESPECT FOR MANY CULTURES
=====================================================

## What you will learn
• Take part in a school game or sports skill for enjoyment.
• Appreciate teamwork and safety in the performance.
• Explain why Creative Arts from many backgrounds are valued.

Curriculum outcomes: e) participate in games and sports within the school for enjoyment; f) value appreciation of Creative Arts works drawn from various cultural backgrounds

## Introduction
Appreciation is not only for songs and pictures. A netball pass, a sprint, a gymnastics sequence, a float or an animal game can be analysed too. You look for teamwork and for safety, and you still enjoy the play.

## Notes
This lesson puts you inside the work you are appreciating. Take part in one game or skill your class can do safely at school: a short sprint with a fair start, chest passes and catching in netball, a crab balance and side roll, a shallow-water skill if your school has a supervised pool, or an indigenous animal game. The aim is enjoyment and good performance, not a quarrel about who is best.

### What to appreciate in sports
- **Teamwork:** passes that reach a teammate, runners who stay in their lanes, a hen and chicks who move together, a group that rotates roles.
- **Safety:** warm-up, clear space, no pushing, feet-first water entry if you are at a pool, and a stop when the whistle goes.
- **Sportsmanship:** honest results, no mocking, help for someone who falls, and a clap at the end. That is integrity.

After you play, analyse in a group. “Our passes were accurate and we stopped on the whistle” is analysis. “We were the best school in the country” is a boast you cannot prove.

### Works from many backgrounds
In one term you may have met a folk song from a community that is not yours, a national anthem that belongs to every Kenyan, a photograph of ordinary school life, and a game passed on through local play. Valuing them means you do not rank cultures from best to worst. You learn the right behaviour for each work: silence for a solemn song, energy for a game, clean hands for a portfolio.

Enjoyment and respect fit together. You can cheer a race and still refuse to laugh at the last runner. You can love your own community’s song and still learn a song from another Kenyan community with care. That is appreciation of Creative Arts drawn from various cultural backgrounds.

## Key words
• teamwork — people working together toward the same aim
• sportsmanship — fair and respectful behaviour in games
• integrity — honesty and doing what is right even when you want to win

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A runner false-starts and then says, “Do not count it, I am the fastest.” What value is missing?

Working:
1. Results should be honest.
2. Integrity and sportsmanship require accepting the rule.

Answer: Integrity, or sportsmanship. The false start has to be accepted.

### Example 2
A class plays 3 short games and each game lasts 5 minutes. How many minutes do they play?

Working:
1. 3 × 5 = 15

Answer: 15 minutes

## Activity: Play and appreciate
You will need: A safe space, Equipment for one familiar game, such as a ball, mats or a marked lane, Whistle
1. Warm up and agree the safety rules.
2. Play a short game or practise a skill for enjoyment. Rotate so everyone takes part.
3. Stop on the whistle.
4. In groups, comment on teamwork and safety using “I noticed…”.
5. Name one Creative Arts work from a culture or community you want to treat with more care, and say how.

## Practice
1. Name two things to appreciate in a sports performance.
2. What is sportsmanship?
3. Why should Creative Arts from different cultural backgrounds be valued?

## Summary
• Take part in games for enjoyment, with teamwork and safety.
• Analyse what you played instead of only claiming to be the best.
• Give the same respect to Creative Arts from every cultural background.

### Answers to practice
1. Teamwork and safety. Sportsmanship may also be named.
2. Fair and respectful behaviour in games.
3. Each carries meaning and skill. Appreciation does not rank communities from best to worst.

studyPages.title: Overview
studyPages.body:
OVERVIEW
========

Appreciation means looking, listening and responding to Creative Arts with care. In this sub-strand you will explain what appreciation includes, make a portfolio for your artworks, and study the Kenya National Anthem and a Kenyan folk song. You will also take part in games and sports and talk about teamwork, safety and works from different cultures.

## Strand 3.0: Appreciation in Creative Arts
Sub-strand 3.1: Analysis of Creative Arts Works
Suggested lessons: 15

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) explain the concept of appreciation in Creative Arts
b) make a portfolio for presenting creative art works
c) analyse the Kenya National Anthem to foster patriotism
d) describe a Kenyan folk song performance using appropriate terminologies
e) participate in games and sports within the school for enjoyment
f) value appreciation of Creative Arts works drawn from various cultural backgrounds

## What this sub-strand covers
• Making a portfolio
• Concept of appreciation: appropriate behaviour, aesthetic, skills, message communicated, how to give feedback, care of displayed works
• Kenya National Anthem; role, values, occasions and number of verses performed
• Components of a folk song: community of origin Type/ occasion, Message, participants and their roles (soloist, instrumentalist, singers), instruments

## Key inquiry questions
1. What is the importance of analysis in Creative Arts?

## Core competencies
• Citizenship: The learner gets to appreciate Kenyan music as they listen to and analyse Kenyan National Anthem and folk songs
• Learning to learn: The learner gets to interact with different type of Creative Arts works gaining new knowledge
• Digital Literacy: The learner appreciates different works of art displayed through multimedia

## Values
• Unity: The learner collaborates with others when analysing in groups the execution of sports skills
• Respect: The learner appreciates others while analysing Creative Arts works in groups
• Integrity: The learner observes sportsmanship during mini games
• Patriotism: The learner develops the love for Kenya as they discuss aspects of the Kenya National Anthem

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Health and safety: The learner participates in sports activities for enjoyment and fun
• Social cohesion: The learner analyses in groups the execution of sports skills in inter class/inter school championships
• Analytical and creative thinking: The learner analyses music and sports events and critiques art works
• Cultural awareness: The learner analyses folk songs from different parts of the Kenya

## Links to other learning areas
• Social Studies: The learner integrates with others while undertaking various tasks in groups
• English: The learner enhances their listening and speaking skills in English while discussing the music listened to

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Creative Arts Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 3.0 Appreciation in Creative Arts, Sub-strand 3.1 Analysis of Creative Arts Works

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: What appreciation means
studyPages.body:
LESSON 1: WHAT APPRECIATION MEANS
=================================

## What you will learn
• Explain appreciation in Creative Arts.
• Name the parts of appreciation: behaviour, beauty, skill, message, feedback and care.
• Show appropriate behaviour while looking at or listening to a work.

Curriculum outcomes: a) explain the concept of appreciation in Creative Arts

## Introduction
Finishing a picture, a song or a race is not the last step. Someone has to look or listen properly. That careful attention, and the fair words that follow it, is appreciation.

## Notes
Appreciation in Creative Arts means giving a work your full attention and responding to it with respect. The work might be a drawing, a painting, a photograph, a song, a folk dance or a sports performance. Analysis is the part of appreciation where you separate the work into pieces so you can understand it. Analysis matters because it helps you see the message, improve your own work, and respect the person who made or performed the work.

In this sub-strand, appreciation includes six ideas.

- **Appropriate behaviour:** sit or stand where you can see and hear. Do not touch a display unless you are allowed to. Do not talk over a song. Do not laugh at a performer.
- **Aesthetic:** the beauty and organisation of the work, such as colour, neatness, balance and a pleasing sound.
- **Skills:** what the maker or performer was able to do, such as a steady balance, a clean pitch or a well-lit photograph.
- **Message:** what the work is communicating.
- **Feedback:** comments that help, given kindly.
- **Care of displayed works:** keeping artworks clean, dry and unharmed.

You do not have to like everything. Appreciation is not pretending. It is being able to say what you noticed and why, without insulting the maker. A useful sentence is: “I notice… and it makes me think…”

When the class listens to a short song or looks at a painting, fold your arms or rest your hands so you are not tempted to touch. Wait until the work is finished. Then speak. That behaviour is the doorway to every other kind of appreciation.

## Key words
• appreciation — giving a work full attention and responding with respect
• analysis — looking at the parts of a work so you can understand it
• aesthetic — to do with beauty and how pleasing a work looks or sounds

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner talks all through a folk song and then says they appreciated it. What is missing?

Working:
1. Appreciation includes appropriate behaviour.
2. Talking over the song means they did not attend to it.

Answer: Appropriate behaviour. They did not listen, so they cannot yet claim to have appreciated the song.

### Example 2
Why is analysis useful?

Working:
1. Analysis separates a work into parts.
2. Those parts reveal the message and the skills.

Answer: It helps you understand the message, improve your own work and respect the maker.

## Activity: Attend, then speak
You will need: One displayed picture and one short recorded song, Exercise books
1. Brainstorm what appreciation means and list the six ideas.
2. Look at the picture in silence for one minute. Do not touch it.
3. Listen to the song in silence.
4. Write “I notice… and it makes me think…” for each work.
5. Share one sentence and let the next person finish before you speak.

## Practice
1. What is appreciation in Creative Arts?
2. Name three things appreciation includes.
3. Why is analysis important?

## Summary
• Appreciation is careful attention and a respectful response.
• It includes behaviour, beauty, skill, message, feedback and care.
• Analysis helps you understand a work instead of only saying you like it.

### Answers to practice
1. Giving a work your full attention and responding to it with respect.
2. Any three: appropriate behaviour, aesthetic qualities, skills, message, feedback, care of displayed works.
3. It helps you understand the message, improve your own work and respect the maker or performer.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Aesthetic qualities, skills and message
studyPages.body:
LESSON 2: AESTHETIC QUALITIES, SKILLS AND MESSAGE
=================================================

## What you will learn
• Comment on the look or sound of a work.
• Name a skill used to make or perform it.
• Suggest a message the work communicates.

Curriculum outcomes: a) explain the concept of appreciation in Creative Arts

## Introduction
“It is nice” does not tell a painter, a singer or a runner anything they can use. Separating beauty, skill and message gives you something true to say.

## Notes
Use three questions on any Creative Arts work.

### What is aesthetic here?
Aesthetic questions are about the senses. In a picture: Are the colours clear? Is the work neat? Is there a balance between the parts? In a photograph: Is the light helping, and is the centre of interest easy to see? In music: Is the tone pleasant? Do the voices match? In gymnastics or sport: Is the body shape clear and controlled? You are describing beauty and organisation, not guessing the price of the work.

### What skill was used?
Skill is what someone has learnt to do. A neat Kenyan flag shows painting skill and knowledge of colour order. A side roll in a straight line shows body control. A recorder melody on B, A and G shows fingering and breath. A pass in netball shows eye and hand skill. Name the skill you can actually see or hear. Do not praise a skill that was not in the performance.

### What message is communicated?
The message is the idea the work carries. A topical song may say “keep the compound clean”. The national anthem carries a message of unity and service. A folk song may advise, mourn, celebrate or call people to work. A sports performance can communicate teamwork even without words. If you are not sure of the message, say “I think the message is…” and give your reason.

Write the three answers in a table with the headings Aesthetic, Skill and Message. A full appreciation uses all three columns. One column alone is only a fragment.

Respect the limits of what you know. If a song is in a language you do not understand, you may comment on the sound, the skill and the occasion, and ask someone from that community about the message instead of inventing it.

## Key words
• skill — something a person has learnt to do well
• message — the idea a work communicates

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A photograph shows a well-lit pot in the middle of a plain background. Give one aesthetic comment and one skill comment.

Working:
1. Aesthetic comments describe look.
2. Skill comments describe what the photographer managed to do.

Answer: Aesthetic: the pot is clear and the background is calm. Skill: the photographer used light and chose a centre of interest.

### Example 2
Learners laugh at the words of a song they do not understand and invent a rude meaning. What should they do instead?

Working:
1. Do not invent a message.
2. Ask someone who knows the language.

Answer: Comment on the sound and the skill, and ask a person from that community what the song means.

## Activity: Three-column analysis
You will need: A displayed artwork, A short performance or recording, A table with three columns
1. Choose one artwork and one performance.
2. Fill Aesthetic, Skill and Message for each.
3. Compare tables with a partner and change any comment that has no evidence.
4. Underline the comment you are most sure of.
5. Ask one question about anything you could not interpret.

## Practice
1. What kind of comment is “the colours are neat and the shapes are balanced”?
2. What is the difference between a skill and a message?
3. What should you do if you do not understand the language of a song?

## Summary
• Ask what is beautiful or well organised, what skill was used, and what message is carried.
• Base each answer on something you can see or hear.
• Do not invent a meaning for a language you do not know.

### Answers to practice
1. An aesthetic comment.
2. A skill is what the person is able to do. A message is the idea the work communicates.
3. Do not invent the meaning. Comment on what you can hear and ask someone who knows the language.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Feedback and care of displayed works
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: FEEDBACK AND CARE OF DISPLAYED WORKS
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Give feedback that is kind, specific and useful.
• Show how to care for works on display.
• Explain why works from different cultures deserve the same care.

Curriculum outcomes: a) explain the concept of appreciation in Creative Arts; f) value appreciation of Creative Arts works drawn from various cultural backgrounds

## Introduction
Feedback can help a classmate improve, or it can make them never want to show work again. Care of a display can keep a painting alive for the whole school, or destroy it in a minute.

## Notes
### How to give feedback
Use this order.

1. Say what you noticed, using aesthetic quality, skill or message.
2. Say what worked.
3. Offer one suggestion, not a list of five.
4. Stop talking and let the maker reply.

A strong example: “I noticed a straight side roll. The body control worked well. Next time, hold the crab balance a little longer.”

A weak example: “It was bad.” It has no detail and no respect.

Do not compare a learner cruelly with a friend. Do not shout feedback across the room. In a group, each person speaks once before anyone speaks twice. That fairness is part of respect.

### Care of displayed works
- Dry paintings before they are stacked.
- Handle paper by the edges.
- Do not write on someone else’s work.
- Keep water, food and dirty hands away from displays.
- Fasten work with tape or clips that the teacher provides, not with pins through the middle of a picture.
- Put sculptures and portfolios where they will not be kicked.
- If you must move a display, ask first.

### Different cultural backgrounds
A painting of a community ceremony, a folk song, or a game from another Kenyan community is not less important than work from your own. Care and feedback stay the same. Laughing at clothing, language or style in a display is not analysis. Valuing works from many backgrounds means you give them the same silence, the same careful hands and the same honest, kind words.

Write one feedback comment you would be willing to hear about your own work. If you would not want to hear it, do not say it to someone else.

## Key words
• feedback — a response that says what worked and one way to improve
• display — work put where others can see it

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Rewrite “Your flag is messy and silly” as useful feedback.

Working:
1. Notice one real point.
2. Say what worked, then one suggestion.

Answer: Example: “I noticed the three wide stripes. The black stripe at the top works. Next time, let each colour dry so the edges stay neat.”

### Example 2
A learner pins a drawing through the middle so it will not fall. What is the problem?

Working:
1. The pin damages the work.
2. Edges or clips should be used instead.

Answer: The pin makes a hole in the picture. Fasten it at the edges or ask the teacher for a clip.

## Activity: Feedback and a safe display
You will need: Two artworks or photographs, Space to display them, Clips or tape
1. Display the works without damaging them.
2. Each learner gives one feedback comment using the four-step order.
3. The maker replies with “thank you” and may ask one question.
4. Check hands are clean and the works are away from food and water.
5. Discuss how you would give the same care to a work from a community that is not your own.

## Practice
1. What are the four steps of useful feedback?
2. Give two ways to care for a displayed painting.
3. Why should works from another culture receive the same care?

## Summary
• Feedback notices something, names a strength and offers one suggestion.
• Handle displays by the edges and keep them clean and dry.
• Give the same respect to works from every cultural background.

### Answers to practice
1. Say what you noticed, say what worked, offer one suggestion, and let the maker reply.
2. Any two: let it dry, handle the edges, keep food and water away, do not write on it, do not pin through the middle.
3. They are equally worth respecting. Appreciation does not rank communities.

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: Making a portfolio
studyPages.body:
LESSON 4: MAKING A PORTFOLIO
============================

## What you will learn
• Explain what a portfolio is for.
• Make a simple portfolio from local materials.
• Decorate it and place artwork inside without damage.

Curriculum outcomes: b) make a portfolio for presenting creative art works

## Introduction
Loose drawings in a desk get torn, and nobody can find the one worth showing. A portfolio is a made container that keeps Creative Arts work together and ready to present.

## Notes
A portfolio is a folder or case that holds your Creative Arts work. A **working portfolio** collects work while you are still learning: sketches, photographs, notes and unfinished ideas. A **display portfolio** holds the work you have chosen to show. In Grade 4 you can make one strong folder that does both jobs.

### Materials
Use what is available: a large piece of manila paper, two pieces of cardboard from a clean box, or a folded chart. You also need glue or tape, and coloured paper or scraps of fabric for decoration. Do not cut up a book or someone else’s work to get the cardboard.

### Steps
1. Cut or fold the cover so it is bigger than the artwork. A folder that is too small bends the pictures.
2. Join the sides and the bottom, and leave the top open. If you glue the top as well, you cannot get the work in.
3. Decorate the front by pasting coloured paper or fabric. Leave a space to write your name, your class and the words “Creative Arts portfolio”.
4. Let the glue dry before you put work inside.
5. Slide artwork in carefully. A painting must be dry. A photograph should be flat.
6. You may write a small label on a separate strip: “Kenyan flag, painted in class”, not across the picture itself.

### Presenting
When you present the portfolio, take out one work at a time, say its title, and use the appreciation language you have learnt. Then put it back. Do not empty the folder onto the floor.

A portfolio shows responsibility. It also lets a teacher see progress, because early work and later work can sit together. Care for it as you care for a display: clean hands, no food inside, and a safe shelf.

## Key words
• portfolio — a folder that keeps and presents Creative Arts work
• working portfolio — a collection of work still in progress
• display portfolio — a collection of work chosen to be shown

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner glues all four edges of the folder. What goes wrong?

Working:
1. The artwork has to go in through an opening.
2. Gluing every edge leaves no opening.

Answer: There is no way to put the artwork inside. One edge, usually the top, must stay open.

### Example 2
The cover is 30 cm wide and the painting is 34 cm wide. Will the painting fit without bending?

Working:
1. 34 is greater than 30.
2. The cover needs to be bigger than the work.

Answer: No. The cover is smaller than the painting, so the painting would bend.

## Activity: Build and fill a portfolio
You will need: Manila paper or clean cardboard, Glue or tape, Coloured paper or fabric scraps, Dry artwork
1. Make a folder bigger than your artwork, with the top open.
2. Decorate the front with coloured paper or fabric and write your name.
3. Let it dry.
4. Place one dry artwork inside and add a separate label.
5. Present that one work to a partner, then return it to the portfolio.

## Practice
1. What is a portfolio for?
2. Which edge of a simple folder should stay open?
3. When is it safe to put a painting into the portfolio?

## Summary
• A portfolio keeps work and helps you present it.
• Make it from local materials, decorate it, and leave an opening.
• Put in dry, flat work and handle it with clean hands.

### Answers to practice
1. To keep Creative Arts work safe and to present chosen work.
2. The top, so artwork can go in.
3. When the paint is dry.

studyPages.title: Lesson 5: The Kenya National Anthem: role, occasions and verses
studyPages.body:
LESSON 5: THE KENYA NATIONAL ANTHEM: ROLE, OCCASIONS AND VERSES
============================================================

## What you will learn
• State the role of the Kenya National Anthem.
• Name occasions when it is performed.
• Recognise that a full performance has three verses.

Curriculum outcomes: c) analyse the Kenya National Anthem to foster patriotism

## Introduction
When the Kenya National Anthem begins, people stand. That habit has a reason. The anthem is one of the ways the country recognises itself.

## Notes
The Kenya National Anthem is the official patriotic song of Kenya. Its Kiswahili title is Ee Mungu Nguvu Yetu. The tune comes from a traditional Pokomo lullaby. The anthem was adopted in 1963, when Kenya became independent. It is sung in Kiswahili and in English.

### Role
The anthem identifies the nation. It asks for blessing, justice, unity, peace and plenty, and it calls citizens to serve and to build the country. Standing for it shows respect. It is a sign of patriotism, not background music.

### Occasions
It is performed at school assemblies, at flag-raising ceremonies, on national days, and when Kenya is represented at international events. National days include Madaraka Day on 1 June, Mashujaa Day on 20 October and Jamhuri Day on 12 December.

### Three verses
A full performance has **three verses**. Each verse has six lines. Some assemblies sing the first verse when time is short, but you should know that the complete anthem has three, and you should be able to listen to all three with attention.

**Verse 1** is a prayer: “O God of all creation, bless this our land and nation…” It asks for justice, unity, peace, liberty and plenty.

**Verse 2** calls everyone to service: “Let one and all arise with hearts both strong and true…” It speaks of defending the homeland.

**Verse 3** calls people to build the nation together and to be thankful: “Let all with one accord in common bond united…”

### Behaviour
Stand still, face the flag if there is one, and stop talking before the first note. Caps come off. You sing if you know the words, or you stand in respectful silence. You do not walk, chew or laugh. When the three verses end, you wait for the signal before you move. That behaviour is part of analysing the anthem as a national symbol, not only as a tune.

## Key words
• national anthem — the official patriotic song of a country
• verse — one section of a song
• patriotism — love and respect for one’s country

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A performance includes verse 1 and verse 2 only. How many verses of the full anthem were left out?

Working:
1. The full anthem has 3 verses.
2. 3 − 2 = 1

Answer: 1

### Example 2
On which date is Jamhuri Day?

Working:
1. Jamhuri Day is a known national day.
2. It is 12 December.

Answer: 12 December.

## Activity: Listen to the three verses
You will need: A recording or a live singing of all three verses of the Kenya National Anthem, The flag if the school has one
1. Stand in silence and listen to all three verses.
2. After the anthem, sit and say what each verse is mainly about.
3. List two occasions when the anthem is performed.
4. Discuss the role it plays for the country.
5. Practise the correct standing position once more as the first verse is played.

## Practice
1. How many verses does the full Kenya National Anthem have?
2. Give two occasions when it is performed.
3. What is one role of the anthem?

## Summary
• The anthem is Kenya’s official patriotic song, adopted in 1963.
• A full performance has three verses.
• Stand still and give it your attention on national and school occasions.

### Answers to practice
1. Three.
2. Any two: school assemblies, flag ceremonies, Madaraka Day, Mashujaa Day, Jamhuri Day, international events where Kenya is represented.
3. It identifies the nation and expresses patriotism, unity and respect.

studyPages.title: Lesson 6: Values in the Kenya National Anthem
studyPages.body:
LESSON 6: VALUES IN THE KENYA NATIONAL ANTHEM
=============================================

## What you will learn
• Find values named in the three verses.
• Explain how those values build patriotism.
• Connect one value to behaviour at school.

Curriculum outcomes: c) analyse the Kenya National Anthem to foster patriotism

## Introduction
The anthem is not only a tune to stand up for. Its words tell citizens how to live with one another. Finding those values is analysis.

## Notes
Listen again, this time for values. A value is a belief about what is right and worth protecting.

### Verse 1
The prayer asks for **justice** (“Justice be our shield and defender”), **unity** (“May we dwell in unity”), **peace**, **liberty** and **plenty**. Justice means fairness. Unity means staying together. Peace means living without harming one another. Liberty means freedom. Plenty means enough for people to live.

### Verse 2
“Service be our earnest endeavour” names **service**, which is working for others and for the country. “Firm may we stand to defend” names **courage** and responsibility for the homeland. The verse asks for strong, true hearts. That is sincerity, not showing off.

### Verse 3
“In common bond united” returns to unity. “Build this our nation together” names **hard work** and cooperation. “Fill every heart with thanksgiving” names **gratitude**. The glory of the country is described as the fruit of labour, so the anthem does not promise pride without effort.

Taken together, the anthem fosters patriotism by giving love of country a practical meaning: be fair, stay united, keep the peace, serve, work and be thankful.

### At school
You practise these values in small ways. Unity is singing together and playing as a team. Justice is taking turns. Service is tidying the space after art or games. Peace is refusing to mock a performance. Gratitude is thanking the person who taught you a song. Patriotism is standing properly for the anthem and treating the flag with care.

When you analyse the anthem, quote or point to the line that carries the value. “I like verse 2” is an opinion. “Verse 2 asks for service” is analysis.

## Key words
• value — a belief about what is right and worth protecting
• justice — fairness
• unity — being together as one people

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which value is clearest in the line “May we dwell in unity”?

Working:
1. The line uses the word unity.
2. Dwelling in unity means living together as one.

Answer: Unity.

### Example 2
A learner says verse 3 is about thanksgiving but cannot point to a line. What should they add?

Working:
1. Analysis points to the words.
2. Verse 3 speaks of filling every heart with thanksgiving.

Answer: They should point to the line about filling every heart with thanksgiving.

## Activity: Match lines to values
You will need: The three verses written where the class can see them, Cards labelled Unity, Justice, Service, Hard work, Thanksgiving, Peace
1. Listen to or read the three verses again.
2. In groups, match each value card to a line.
3. Explain the match in one sentence.
4. Choose one value and say how you can practise it at school this week.
5. Stand and sing or listen to verse 1 with the value of unity in mind.

## Practice
1. Name three values found in the Kenya National Anthem.
2. Which verse especially calls people to serve and defend the homeland?
3. Give one way to practise unity at school.

## Summary
• Verse 1 prays for justice, unity, peace, liberty and plenty.
• Verse 2 calls for service. Verse 3 calls for shared work and thanksgiving.
• Patriotism here means living those values, including at school.

### Answers to practice
1. Any three: justice, unity, peace, liberty, service, hard work, gratitude or thanksgiving, patriotism.
2. Verse 2.
3. Any one: sing together, take turns, play as a team, listen to one another.

studyPages.title: Lesson 7: Describing a Kenyan folk song
studyPages.body:
LESSON 7: DESCRIBING A KENYAN FOLK SONG
=======================================

## What you will learn
• Describe a folk song using community, occasion, message, participants and instruments.
• Use the words soloist, instrumentalist and singers correctly.
• Avoid guessing facts you did not see or hear.

Curriculum outcomes: d) describe a Kenyan folk song performance using appropriate terminologies

## Introduction
A good description of a folk song is like a good description of a match. You name who took part, what they did, and what the event was for. Feelings come after the facts.

## Notes
When you analyse a Kenyan folk song performance, use these components.

- **Community of origin:** which community the song comes from. If you do not know, write “not yet identified” and ask. Do not guess from the costumes alone.
- **Type or occasion:** work, funeral, naming, initiation, marriage, worship, or another occasion you can support from the performance or from a reliable person.
- **Message:** what the song is saying or doing for the people at that occasion. Ask if the language is not yours.
- **Participants and their roles:** the **soloist** leads, the **singers** answer or join the tune, and the **instrumentalist** plays. One person might dance as well. Name the roles you actually saw.
- **Instruments:** drums, kayamba, shakers, or body percussion such as clapping. Name only the instruments you heard.

A clear description sounds like this: “This was isukuti from Luhya communities, especially associated with the Isukha and Idakho. It is performed at joyful occasions such as weddings. I saw drummers, who were the instrumentalists, and dancers who also sang. The message I could confirm is celebration. I would need a speaker of the language to explain every line.”

That is appropriate terminology. Words such as “nice”, “funny clothes” or “noise” are not analysis.

Compare two songs only when you have the components for both. You may find that a work song and a marriage song use different speeds and different messages, and that both deserve respect. Cultural awareness grows when the description is accurate.

## Key words
• soloist — the person who leads the singing
• instrumentalist — the person who plays an instrument
• community of origin — the community the song comes from

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A report says, “The song was noisy and from somewhere.” What is missing?

Working:
1. A description needs components.
2. Community, occasion, roles and instruments are missing, and the tone is disrespectful.

Answer: It does not name the community, the occasion, the message, the roles or the instruments.

### Example 2
Three people hit drums and one person leads the singing while ten people answer. Who is the soloist?

Working:
1. The soloist leads the singing.
2. The drummers are instrumentalists.

Answer: The person who leads the singing.

## Activity: Analyse one performance
You will need: A live or recorded Kenyan folk song, A component chart
1. Watch or listen once without writing.
2. Watch again and fill: community, occasion, message, soloist, singers, instrumentalists, instruments.
3. Leave a box blank rather than guessing.
4. Share the chart with another group and challenge any fact that was not in the performance.
5. Write two sentences of appreciation using the correct terms.

## Practice
1. List five components used to describe a folk song performance.
2. What does the instrumentalist do?
3. What should you write if you do not know the community of origin?

## Summary
• Describe community, occasion, message, roles and instruments.
• Use the terms soloist, singers and instrumentalist.
• Leave out any fact you cannot support.

### Answers to practice
1. Community of origin, type or occasion, message, participants and their roles, and instruments.
2. Plays an instrument.
3. “Not yet identified,” and then ask. Do not guess.

studyPages.title: Lesson 8: Games, sports and respect for many cultures
studyPages.body:
LESSON 8: GAMES, SPORTS AND RESPECT FOR MANY CULTURES
=====================================================

## What you will learn
• Take part in a school game or sports skill for enjoyment.
• Appreciate teamwork and safety in the performance.
• Explain why Creative Arts from many backgrounds are valued.

Curriculum outcomes: e) participate in games and sports within the school for enjoyment; f) value appreciation of Creative Arts works drawn from various cultural backgrounds

## Introduction
Appreciation is not only for songs and pictures. A netball pass, a sprint, a gymnastics sequence, a float or an animal game can be analysed too. You look for teamwork and for safety, and you still enjoy the play.

## Notes
This lesson puts you inside the work you are appreciating. Take part in one game or skill your class can do safely at school: a short sprint with a fair start, chest passes and catching in netball, a crab balance and side roll, a shallow-water skill if your school has a supervised pool, or an indigenous animal game. The aim is enjoyment and good performance, not a quarrel about who is best.

### What to appreciate in sports
- **Teamwork:** passes that reach a teammate, runners who stay in their lanes, a hen and chicks who move together, a group that rotates roles.
- **Safety:** warm-up, clear space, no pushing, feet-first water entry if you are at a pool, and a stop when the whistle goes.
- **Sportsmanship:** honest results, no mocking, help for someone who falls, and a clap at the end. That is integrity.

After you play, analyse in a group. “Our passes were accurate and we stopped on the whistle” is analysis. “We were the best school in the country” is a boast you cannot prove.

### Works from many backgrounds
In one term you may have met a folk song from a community that is not yours, a national anthem that belongs to every Kenyan, a photograph of ordinary school life, and a game passed on through local play. Valuing them means you do not rank cultures from best to worst. You learn the right behaviour for each work: silence for a solemn song, energy for a game, clean hands for a portfolio.

Enjoyment and respect fit together. You can cheer a race and still refuse to laugh at the last runner. You can love your own community’s song and still learn a song from another Kenyan community with care. That is appreciation of Creative Arts drawn from various cultural backgrounds.

## Key words
• teamwork — people working together toward the same aim
• sportsmanship — fair and respectful behaviour in games
• integrity — honesty and doing what is right even when you want to win

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A runner false-starts and then says, “Do not count it, I am the fastest.” What value is missing?

Working:
1. Results should be honest.
2. Integrity and sportsmanship require accepting the rule.

Answer: Integrity, or sportsmanship. The false start has to be accepted.

### Example 2
A class plays 3 short games and each game lasts 5 minutes. How many minutes do they play?

Working:
1. 3 × 5 = 15

Answer: 15 minutes

## Activity: Play and appreciate
You will need: A safe space, Equipment for one familiar game, such as a ball, mats or a marked lane, Whistle
1. Warm up and agree the safety rules.
2. Play a short game or practise a skill for enjoyment. Rotate so everyone takes part.
3. Stop on the whistle.
4. In groups, comment on teamwork and safety using “I noticed…”.
5. Name one Creative Arts work from a culture or community you want to treat with more care, and say how.

## Practice
1. Name two things to appreciate in a sports performance.
2. What is sportsmanship?
3. Why should Creative Arts from different cultural backgrounds be valued?

## Summary
• Take part in games for enjoyment, with teamwork and safety.
• Analyse what you played instead of only claiming to be the best.
• Give the same respect to Creative Arts from every cultural background.

### Answers to practice
1. Teamwork and safety. Sportsmanship may also be named.
2. Fair and respectful behaviour in games.
3. Each carries meaning and skill. Appreciation does not rank communities from best to worst.

questions.question: Appreciation in Creative Arts means…
options: giving a work attention and responding with respect
questions.explanation: Appreciation is careful attention and a respectful response.

questions.question: Which comment is about aesthetic quality?
questions.explanation: Aesthetic comments describe beauty and organisation.

questions.question: Useful feedback includes…
options: what you noticed, what worked, and one suggestion
a joke about the maker’s clothes
a pin through the middle of the picture
questions.explanation: Feedback is specific, kind and limited to one suggestion.

questions.question: A portfolio is used to…
options: keep and present Creative Arts work
mark the deep end of a pool
questions.explanation: A portfolio holds work safely and helps you show it.

questions.question: Before a wet painting goes into a portfolio it must…
questions.explanation: Wet paint smears and damages the portfolio and the picture.

questions.question: How many verses does the full Kenya National Anthem have?
questions.explanation: A full performance has three verses.

questions.question: Which value is named by “May we dwell in unity”?
questions.explanation: The line asks the nation to live in unity.

questions.question: Jamhuri Day is on…
questions.explanation: Jamhuri Day, Independence Day, is 12 December.

questions.question: Which set names components of a folk song performance?
options: Head joint, middle joint, foot joint
questions.explanation: Folk-song analysis uses community, occasion, message, participants and instruments.

questions.question: The soloist in a folk song is the person who…
questions.explanation: The soloist sings the leading part.

questions.question: In a game, good sportsmanship means…
options: ignoring a false start because you want to win
playing fairly and treating others with respect
refusing to stop for the whistle
questions.explanation: Sportsmanship is fair and respectful play.

questions.question: Why should a class value Creative Arts from communities other than their own?
questions.answer: Those works carry meaning and skill, and appreciation does not rank cultures from best to worst.
questions.explanation: Respect applies to works from every cultural background.
